articles.title: ISC2 Launches Cyber-AI Workforce Coalition to Address the Future of AI Security Jobs
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
After years of tracking the global cybersecurity skills gap through its annual Cybersecurity Workforce Study, ISC2 is taking a more active role in shaping the future of the profession with the launch of its Cyber-AI Workforce Coalition.

Announced on October 20, the new coalition is one of the first major developments introduced by Scott Beale, ISC2’s CEO, who took on the role in December 2025.

Speaking to Infosecurity during the ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Beale said he spent his first six months as CEO listening to the organization’s members.

A key finding from the consultation was that a majority of ISC2 members want the nonprofit to more ambitiously and vocally step into the AI safety and security space.

“We want to be the association that can help prepare the cybersecurity workforce for the many challenges of this AI era,” Beale added.

Mapping the AI Security Workforce and Its Emerging Skills Gap

Beale described the coalition as a “vendor-neutral convener” for global cybersecurity professionals. It aims to include thought leaders like HR managers and CISOs, some of the largest employers of cybersecurity practitioners, standard-setting bodies and even government representatives to discuss how cybersecurity roles are changing because of AI.

“Even as the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and others are updating standards and frameworks, companies are still facing a lack of resources for how to best advertise and fill these roles. How a bank describes these jobs is still very different from how a hospital would,” Beale said.

Hiring needs at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity remain uncertain, according to Beale. There remain unanswered questions about how AI will affect future demand for cybersecurity professionals, which skills will be most critical for AI security roles, and how experienced practitioners can upskill to meet emerging demands.

“The coalition a way for us to listen directly to these people and help move the sector in a way that can be responsive to their needs,” he said.

Practical Tools to Define and Hire for AI Security Roles

In practice, the coalition will not create new standards or frameworks but will instead focus on delivering toolkits for employers to help them describe new job roles at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity.

These toolkits will include guidance for how employers hire, develop and organize cybersecurity talent, and how practitioners can identify and build the expertise employers need.

These new tools will help answer three main questions:

How are cybersecurity jobs changing?

How are employers writing job descriptions for these new roles?

How are candidates preparing to interview and fill these jobs?

“As you know, ISC2 is working on a new AI security certification, and certainly we think It is going to be part of that answer and will help us define some of these new roles,” he said. “However, by no means do we pretend having the only solution to this problem.”

The coalition will hold its first meeting in November. Beale hopes it can develop its first series of toolkits by the spring of 2027 and have some companies using them in a pilot phase to help them hire AI security professionals.

The tools produced by the coalition are expected to eventually be made available for everyone to use, not just ISC2 members. Beale believes they will also be useful for universities and certification bodies to adapt their curriculums.

articles.title: Introducing the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge
articles.context: We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and...
articles.full_text:
Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First, eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised, creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came php2shell: serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web.

Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and introduced a new feature called full transaction detection.

As always in situations like this, these new capabilities were made available on all plans, including Free.

Put our WAF to the test

Protecting systems from vulnerabilities like these is always an ongoing process, not a one-time event. The widespread adoption of AI allows attackers to discover new vectors with unprecedented speed and efficiency, so collecting real-world data to test our assumptions and strengthen defenses is essential.

That’s why today we're launching the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge, run through our Bug Bounty program. We've put a deliberately vulnerable PHP installation behind our WAF, and we're inviting security researchers on HackerOne to try to bypass the protections and capture a flag.

How this Capture the Flag (CTF) works

We are keeping this simple. The challenge focuses on CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the two PHP vulnerabilities behind php2shell. The target runs stock PHP 8.5.11 (with standard PHP extensions), Apache 2 (via mod_php), and an empty index.php inside a Cloudflare Container, with our default WAF protection rules for these vulnerabilities enabled in front of it. Inside the sandbox is a file called /flag.

The sandbox is reset every few minutes, including the flag file.

Your mission, should you choose to accept it: bypass the WAF protections, exploit the PHP sandbox, and recover the contents of /flag. You can use your own research tools. The challenge page has the environment details, scope, and flag verification form.

Challenge requirements

This limited-time challenge is run via Cloudflare's Bug Bounty program on HackerOne. All aspects of this challenge are subject to HackerOne terms and the Cloudflare HackerOne program rules the (“Bounty Terms”). If you find an eligible bypass, you must follow these requirements in order to claim the bounty:

All participants must sign up for a HackerOne account and review and agree to the Bounty Terms before participating in the CTF.

Demonstrate attacker-controlled PHP code or command execution inside the sandbox through an authorized POST request.

Use that remote code execution (RCE) to recover the current contents of /flag, then successfully verify the flag through the CTF user interface (UI). Verify promptly before a reset; retain the successful result for later review.

Submit a private report to Cloudflare on HackerOne. Include PHP CTF in the title and provide:

The endpoint, complete payload, and request sequence, preserving relevant headers, encoding, and body bytes.

Raw request/response captures or a readable proof of concept sufficient to reproduce the full chain.

An explanation of the WAF bypass, executed code or command, and how that execution recovered /flag.

The attempt ID, successful UI verification result, and exploit/verification UTC timestamps. Include the flag privately if needed for verification.

What makes the method or payload materially distinct, and related submissions you know about.

UI verification does not submit a HackerOne report or establish reporting priority. File disclosure without RCE, RCE without successful flag recovery and UI verification, local-only exploits, rediscovery of the known PHP vulnerabilities, and WAF detection differences or partial chains without the full objective are not eligible.

Awards require a materially distinct Firewall (WAF) bypass method, even for the same PHP CVE. Reports using the same Firewall-bypass mechanism are duplicates, regardless of differences in the PHP exploit, payload, RCE technique, or flag-recovery method. New flags, resets, attempt IDs, or cosmetic changes—including equivalent encodings—do not qualify as unique. Equivalent submissions are duplicates even if unfixed; only the first complete, reproducible HackerOne report is considered. Cloudflare makes final duplicate and reward decisions.

We record attempted metadata and request payloads to help analyze reports, so please use test data only. Do not send credentials, personal information, or anything else you would not want included in a research record. Read Cloudflare’s privacy notice before testing.

Testing is authorized only against the challenge hostname's WAF-protected /php/* endpoints (POST method only). Other Cloudflare services, direct access to the underlying infrastructure, the upstream PHP project, and third-party systems are out of scope. No denial of service, high-volume scanning, persistence, social engineering, or attacks on other participants. If you get a 429 or 503, back off.

In the event of any conflict between this blog post and the Bounty Terms, the Bounty Terms shall prevail.

Cloudflare reserves the right to suspend or terminate this challenge at any time. Once the competition is removed from HackerOne, it is officially terminated, so please refer to the Cloudflare HackerOne page for the most up-to-date information on whether this challenge remains open.

Not a substitute for patching

Our WAF protects you, but it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Response blocking can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. If you run PHP, follow the latest PHP security advisories and apply the relevant updates.

Last week was a reminder that helping build a better Internet often takes many people—researchers, maintainers, and teams across the industry—doing difficult, urgent work together.

We hope this challenge gives everyone a useful way to join in. Head over to php-rce.cloudflare.app if you want to participate: the flag is there, and we'd like to know if you can get it.

articles.title: Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF
articles.context: ref Signature reference IDs, up to 10 The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester.

These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shell vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper.

Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error.

With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability.

And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans.

Request inspection is not enough

Cloudflare WAF protects websites and APIs with managed rules, custom rules, and rate limiting. Managed rules provide protection for known attack techniques and vulnerabilities while custom rules let teams create their own policies using parameters such as an IP address, URL path, headers, and request body. These controls operate at the request level to stop exploits or unwanted traffic from reaching the origin.

For many threats, this is the right place to act. However, treating every suspicious request as a confirmed exploit creates a difficult choice. Broad request signatures can catch more potential attacks, but they can also show “false positives”, such as matching legitimate traffic — which then breaks the applications. Deploying only rules that do not trigger false positives reduces that risk, but can leave more room for more ambiguous traffic to reach the server.

The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction.

As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory:

GET /download?file=../../config/database.ini

Request inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence:

200 OK Content-Type: text/plain [database] username=app_service password=EXAMPLE_SECRET

Full transaction detection provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentation or example downloads; combining it with a traversal attempt provides stronger evidence of sensitive data exposure than either signal alone. A response rule can then replace the origin response with a Cloudflare WAF block page and HTTP 403 before it reaches the requester, effectively blocking the exploit by preventing sensitive information from reaching the attacker.

Detection and mitigation are separate by design

Full transaction detection extends the always-on detection framework we introduced earlier this year. Detections analyze traffic and attach metadata to the request and response, rules then decide what to do with those results.

Separating those jobs gives customers visibility before they design a policy. Security teams can inspect detections in their own traffic, understand which endpoints and signatures are involved, and choose the response that fits their application. Similar to the approach for the request-based Attack Signature Detection, the outcome of the detections are stored in fields that can be accessed in the response custom rules or used in managed detections to block traffic.

Mirroring the request detection fields, the following new fields are added to our platform:

Field

Description

cf.waf.signature.response.confidence

Confidence values associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.categories

Categories associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.ref

Signature reference IDs, up to 10

The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability. It correlates suspicious input with response signals that indicate an exploit may have succeeded.

We will expand coverage over time by supporting other use cases, including detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals. This is important for the Internet beyond any one application: defenses can distinguish probing from evidence of impact, while detection of exposed data and services can reach customers that do not have a dedicated security team tuning every WAF rule.

Create rules on the response

Detecting evidence of exploitation is most useful if you can act on it in real time. Response custom rules turn full transaction detections into inline protection by blocking a matching origin response before it reaches the requester, although it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin.

Security teams can now combine request and response properties with detection results to decide which responses to block. When a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response.

Response phase controls are available in the Cloudflare dashboard at the bottom of the Security > Security Rules page, with both managed protections and custom rules.

We have released both managed and custom rules to all plans, including Free plans. Over time, we will follow the same approach we use for request detections, where managed detections for free plans focus on high-profile vulnerabilities, while paying customers get a richer catalog of detections.

Managed detections

All customers get the protection of the full array of transaction detections through the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default ruleset, which is designed for a simple one-click deploy and simplified configurability. When a signature matches, the managed detection will block the response and return a standard WAF block page.

You can edit the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default scope to run detections only on a portion of their applications, for example by excluding or restricting the detection to a specific path. Paying customers can use detection fields in custom response rules to create more tailored policies.

Custom rules

Custom response rules are designed to give customers full control of the rule logic. A useful rule can stop an administration interface from being exposed when an authentication gateway has not marked the request as internal. For example:

http.request.uri.path starts_with "/admin" and not http.request.headers["x-internal-user"][0] eq "true" and http.response.code eq 200 and http.response.headers["content-type"][0] contains "text/html"

This blocks only when an unauthenticated request targets `/admin` and the origin actually returns a successful HTML administration page. It does not block ordinary authentication failures, redirects, or non-administration traffic.

All customers can create up to three custom response rules supporting Log and Block actions. The fields and functions available in response to custom rules mirrors what your plan gives you access to in request custom rules already. Creating rules on the response body is not yet available.

Following the Attack Signature Detection approach, paying customers also have access to the outcome of attack detections through the cf.waf.signature.response.* fields listed above. These fields can be combined with other parameters (such as a hostname, URL path, source IP, request header) to enable protection on a single path, or limit the policy to application-specific context. We are currently rolling out the response fields to all our accounts. If you don’t have access to them yet, please contact your account team.

Investigating matching requests

When a managed or custom response rule logs or blocks a transaction, the event is available in Security Events. This means responders can trace any detection back to the full context of the request and the specific rule that took action.

At the moment, both request-only rules and full-transaction rules are shown together in the same analytics page. In Security Events, the events generated by response rules are part of the Managed Rules or Custom Rules service. You can filter events belonging to a specific rule ID in the relative rule list section.

Get started today

Full transaction detection is generally available for all zones proxying traffic through Cloudflare. To verify that you’re protected, go to Security > Security Rules in the Cloudflare dashboard. If you want to customize your policy, start by reviewing full transaction detections in Security Analytics, then create the response phase policy that fits your application.

articles.title: Shadow AI Detection Now Extends to Developer Workstations
articles.context: ZIP files shared between co-workers containing new agent skills, locally-developed MCP servers passed between developers, and locally stored newly-minted agents are all...
articles.full_text:
ZIP files shared between co-workers containing new agent skills, locally-developed MCP servers passed between developers, and locally stored newly-minted agents are all seemingly harmless files that are commonly used in corporate software development environments.

Unfortunately, far from being harmless, these locally stored files can contain AI assets that were never detected or registered as an approved artifact in your applications.

Such skills are what we refer to as “Shadow AI,” and often they reside on private developer workstations, which are often not governed by central controls. The good news is that you can now detect “local Shadow AI”. By deploying JFrog AI Security, you can extend Shadow AI detection from your repositories to the laptops and workstations where these coding agents actually run, and the work gets done. Let’s break it down.

Ungated Executables: How AI Assets Bypass Security Controls

Until recently, building software followed a strict, secure process: approved code and tools come from trusted official sources, get scanned for vulnerabilities, and must pass company security policies before anyone is allowed to use them.

In today’s “AI-Era”, you can no longer rely on this traditional process for AI assets. Because AI tools and developers can instantly introduce unvetted files, scripts, and plugins on-demand – often straight from GitHub, Slack threads, or even generated by the agent itself – these assets completely bypass standard security checks. This turns a controlled, predictable workflow into something instant, random, and unmonitored.

Some examples include:

Skills: bundles of instructions and scripts that define how an agent performs a task.

MCP servers: Model Context Protocol servers, the connectors that enable agents to interact with systems such as databases, Jira, or Slack.

Plugins: installable packages that bundle skills, MCP servers, and more.

All of these unchecked assets represent serious potential security issues. Perhaps this is best exemplified by Hooks, where authors single-handedly decide what runs on which machine every time the agent is invoked – without ever consulting the rest of the team.

In essence, we wind up with two paths: the Managed Path where assets are scanned and vetted, and the Local Path where Shadow AI components go undetected.

Two paths for AI assets: one governed by JFrog, one with no gates and no reviews

Security Beyond the Repo: Protecting Developer Workstations

Previously, JFrog AI Security detected Shadow AI in your software supply chain by scanning AI models in your JFrog Artifactory repositories and calls to external AI services in your builds. That established a baseline for what we detect in the managed path of your software supply chain, and it worked pretty well, until now.

Shadow AI is more challenging to detect than third-party code and open-source packages, which are introduced into the development environment through a well established centralized build process and not stored on local machines.

Previously, the main risks on developer machines were due to extensions or tools over which DevOps had full control. The risk today is that malicious or non-compliant AI assets, used by coding agents, represent a new type of risk happening autonomously without visibility or control over developer laptops and workstations. This requires an added layer of protection that transparently detects Shadow AI on local machines without affecting developer productivity.

In addition to detecting AI assets on developer machines, JFrog AI Security also provides essential information to security teams and platform administrators regarding potential threats, including:

What risk does it carry? A skill that can run shell commands carries much greater risk than one that can only read files.

Is it allowed by organizational policy? A GitHub MCP server on a laptop may be acceptable if it matches the one you approved, but is a problem if someone built it from a random repository. JFrog plans to add this capability in a future release.

Here is how it works in practice:

Detection is enabled by installing the JFrog Agent Plugin on each developer workstation and operates by following these three steps:

Discover. Detects potentially risky skills, MCP servers, plugins, hooks, commands, and monitors.

Scan Locally. Runs a light deterministic rules-based scan on each workstation where the plugin is installed, designed so that the same input gets the same result every time.

Report. Sends metadata, asset identity, findings, and risk analysis to the JFrog Platform.

How Shadow AI assets on developer workstations become visible

Centralized Visibility Across Managed & Unmanaged AI Assets

JFrog AI Security turns detailed AI asset reports into a single unified inventory. Each record shows the asset’s name, type, harness that reported it (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.), number of workstations where it was detected, local risk analysis, JFrog origin, and detection timestamp.

Two key metrics help prioritize the potential threats to address:

Risk Assessment reveals the underlying security findings for each rating upon selection:

Shell Access + WebFetch: High risk of data exfiltration.

Unscoped Write/Edit: Modifies files outside designated directories.

BypassPermissions Mode: Executes actions without required approval.

Origin documents if the asset already exists in the JFrog Platform:

JFrog Artifactory or JFrog Catalog: The selected asset matches an asset already managed by the JFrog Platform.

No Match: The asset does not match any asset managed in your JFrog Platform.

Gain Complete Visibility Over Your AI Assets

Your developers might already be using AI assets that have not been vetted or approved. Detecting Shadow AI on workstations can help you understand the severity and risk associated with each unmanaged AI asset.

JFrog AI Security ensures managed and unmanaged AI assets follow the same rules as every other artifact you ship: one unified supply chain, one system of record with no Shadow AI exceptions.

articles.title: Introducing ITDR Lookback: Find Out Who Was in Your Microsoft 365 Tenant Before You Were
articles.context: Today, Huntress Managed ITDR's Lookback feature is generally available for newly onboarded Microsoft 365 tenants
articles.full_text:
Today, Huntress Managed ITDR's Lookback feature is generally available for newly onboarded Microsoft 365 tenants. Lookback automatically examines up to 180 days of login history to uncover evidence of compromise before Huntress connected. When a compromise is still active, our Security Operations Center (SOC) investigates and revokes the identity's active sessions.

Onboarding a Microsoft 365 tenant feels like a fresh start. You go through your checklist, and a successful connection tells you monitoring has started. But it doesn't tell you if an attacker got there first. Your first day protecting a tenant might be an attacker's twenty-seventh day inside.

That's what Lookback seeks to solve. You get a clearer picture of the tenant you've inherited, plus defenders who act on what they find. And yes, that includes trial tenants.

Six months of login history. A much stronger start.

Lookback runs once, automatically, when a Microsoft 365 tenant finishes onboarding to Managed ITDR. There's nothing extra to configure and no separate scan to remember to launch.

Huntress Managed ITDR's new Lookback feature is generally available, bringing up to 180 days of Microsoft 365 login history into the hunt for existing compromises.

Lookback applies Huntress's full set of Unwanted Access detections to the tenant's available Microsoft 365 login history, looking back up to 180 days. That includes detections for credential theft, token theft, adversary-in-the-middle attacks, suspicious browsers, and datacenter logins.

Here's the tricky part: evidence of an old compromise doesn't necessarily mean an attacker still has access. Someone may have already reset the password or revoked the compromised sessions. Treating every historical finding as a fresh emergency would make onboarding pretty miserable.

Lookback separates findings based on whether the compromise is still active:

Active compromises receive a critical Incident Report investigated by the Huntress AI-centric SOC, with the identity's active sessions revoked. This turns historical evidence into a reason to act right away.

Previously remediated compromises appear in the Identity Security Assessment as historical context. They don't trigger a new incident or an unnecessary lockdown for something you've already fixed.

That distinction matters. A raw list of suspicious logins leaves the sorting to you. Lookback does it first, so you can see what happened and which parts still need attention.

What's in the report, and where do you find it?

Lookback adds a dedicated section to the Identity Security Assessment, covering compromises that predate Huntress monitoring. It shows the period reviewed and previously remediated incidents, including affected identities, relevant dates, and observed remediation evidence, such as a password reset or session revocation. The report gives you a documented history you can use in a customer conversation or share with leadership.

That history sits alongside the assessment's existing coverage of identities, Rogue Apps, Shadow Workflows such as malicious inbox rules, Unwanted Access, and SOC findings and containment actions. Active compromises uncovered by Lookback also receive their own Incident Reports.

Lookback is part of onboarding for newly connected Microsoft 365 tenants. The assessment is generated automatically after onboarding and waits for Lookback to finish, so you receive one complete document. Once that historical review is complete, Managed ITDR continues monitoring for new threats with the Huntress SOC behind it.

The attackers who arrived before we did

In Lookback's first two weeks of early testing, Huntress reviewed more than 400 tenants. Among them were three very different organizations with the same unwelcome surprise: an active compromise already in progress.

A title company and a $2 million wire

A device-code phishing attack gave an adversary access three days before the tenant onboarded. The attacker persisted through a rogue Entra device and was watching a $2 million real estate wire transfer. Lookback surfaced the active compromise, which Huntress contained.

For a business moving that kind of money, "let's wait until the attacker does something else" is a lousy security strategy.

A school district with an unwanted administrator

A school district's Global Admin account had been compromised 27 days before onboarding. An unrevoked refresh token and a rogue Azure AD device kept the attacker's access alive, with the privileges to control the tenant. Lookback uncovered the compromise, and Huntress contained it. Twenty-seven days is a long head start. Connecting a new security tool shouldn't give the attacker more time simply because the break-in happened earlier.

An architecture firm turned into a phishing launchpad

An architecture firm onboarded with a nine-day foothold still active. The attack involved a hidden inbox rule and 103 external OneDrive phishing invitations sent in a single scripted second. The compromised account had become infrastructure for targeting other people. Lookback surfaced the compromise, which Huntress contained.

In all three cases, the attack began before onboarding. Looking backward gave our defenders evidence to act on right away, without waiting for an attacker's next move.

Less guesswork for you, more proof for your customers

If you're an MSP, every new client brings a history you didn't write. You still have to explain what you've inherited and what you plan to do about it.

Lookback helps you start that relationship with evidence from the client's own environment. You can show past compromises, distinguish resolved activity from active threats, and explain where Huntress has intervened. The shareable assessment makes that conversation easier, while SOC investigation and containment keep the historical review from becoming another helpdesk project.

Internal IT teams get the same benefit. Whether you've inherited a tenant through an acquisition, a vendor change, or staff turnover, you don't have to become a Microsoft audit log specialist to spot signs of prior compromise.

And if you're evaluating Huntress, your trial includes the same Lookback protection as a paid tenant. You can see what we find in your environment and how we respond to active threats while you're still making your decision.

Looking back is how we keep moving forward

Lookback is the latest step in our work to build best-in-class Managed ITDR that earns its place in your security stack every day.

The new ITDR dashboard puts identity activity and investigation tools closer at hand, including Rapid Identity Triage, Failed Login Characterization, and Quick SIEM Search. And the recently released ITDR Executive Summary makes technical incident findings easier to explain to business leaders, with plain-English context about what happened and the response.

Lookback extends that progress into the history you inherit at onboarding. Together, these releases help you understand existing threats, investigate current activity, and explain the work being done to protect the business.

Our standard for innovation is practical: does it help find an attacker, take work off your team, or give you an answer you couldn't easily get before? Lookback delivers on all three, backed by the same 24/7 SOC that protects your identities going forward.

Your tenant has a past, and now you can find out who's still living in it.

Ready to see what came before day one? Start a free trial of Huntress Managed ITDR and connect a Microsoft 365 tenant. Lookback runs automatically, with findings in your Identity Security Assessment and SOC response for active compromises.

articles.title: Huntress + AlgaPSA Integration: Built in Days by Nine Minds
articles.context: Over the past year, the Huntress API has grown from six read-only endpoints into a full integration and automation platform, along with Webhooks and an MCP server
articles.full_text:
Over the past year, the Huntress API has grown from six read-only endpoints into a full integration and automation platform, along with Webhooks and an MCP server. For partners, that means Huntress data can show up wherever they already work, not just in our portal. It also means software vendors can build their own Huntress integrations on their own schedule, without having to wait on us.

Nine Minds is a great example. Their team built a Huntress integration for AlgaPSA, their professional services automation (PSA) platform, using our public API documentation. No technical support or special access needed. They just read the docs and, a few days later, had a working integration. This post covers what they built, what the experience was like, and what it shows about how you can use the Huntress API.

Meet Nine Minds and AlgaPSA

Nine Minds was founded by Robert Isaacs and Arnie Bellini, who both spent over a decade at ConnectWise. AlgaPSA is their answer to a problem they saw in the industry for years: PSA tools that are too expensive, too complicated, and primarily built for mature organizations.

AlgaPSA brings ticketing, projects, time tracking, billing, and client operations into one platform, and it was designed with the smallest MSPs in mind. As Robert told ChannelE2E, "The small MSP doesn't want to sign a three-year contract." But as they've progressed, larger MSPs have started taking notice, too.

AlgaPSA gives MSPs control over how they run the software with hosted, self-hosted, and open-source options. Over a hundred MSPs now rely on AlgaPSA for day-to-day operations, with more signing up every week.

Why Build a Huntress Integration?

For Nine Minds, the decision came down to two things. Mutual customers were asking for it, and their team spends a lot of time in the MSP community, including at IT Nation, and Huntress is one of the names they see everywhere.

When your users already rely on Huntress to catch threats, the next question is simple: how do those incidents get to the technicians who need to act on them? The AlgaPSA <> Huntress integration provides an answer.

How the Integration Works

The integration is built around the premise that a security incident should never go without a ticket. When the Huntress SOC publishes an incident report, it appears in AlgaPSA as a ticket on a dedicated security board, with the incident summary and a priority based on its severity.

Technicians work it like any other ticket, and the time they log flows into AlgaPSA's billing and invoicing. That means security responses get tracked and billed like the rest of their work, instead of living in a separate console. When the SOC closes the incident, the ticket can close automatically, too. And if an incident comes from a client that hasn't been mapped yet, it still lands on a triage board, so nothing slips through.

Setup takes a few steps:

Connect your Huntress API credentials

Map Huntress organizations to AlgaPSA clients

Choose where tickets land and how severities translate to priorities.

Nine Minds walks through each step in the AlgaPSA Huntress integration docs.

A few things to know before you start:

Use a dedicated API key. Huntress API keys are tied to a user and mirror that user's permissions, so it's a good idea to create a separate key just for this integration.

You need AlgaPSA's paid tier. The Huntress integration is part of AlgaPSA's Enterprise Edition (also offered as AlgaPSA Pro). It isn't included in the open-source Community Edition.

Finish routing first. AlgaPSA won't start pulling incidents until the security board, the fallback client and board, and priorities for all three Huntress severities (Critical, High, and Low) are set.

Expect tickets on a schedule, not instantly. AlgaPSA checks Huntress for new incident reports at an interval you choose between one and 60 minutes, so tickets show up at the next check.

What Was It Like to Build on the Huntress API?

This is the part we're most excited about. Nine Minds went from idea to a shipped integration in just a few days.

They built it using our public documentation, without reaching out to us first. After a short period working out which data they needed, Robert said things went smoothly: no confusing fields, no missing endpoints, no documentation gaps that slowed them down. Their team also uses AI coding tools, and pointing those tools at the Huntress API docs was enough to get the job done.

"Integrating Huntress into AlgaPSA was easy enough that we almost felt as if we had missed something... [Then] our customers started thanking us for the integration. Working with Huntress could not have been easier."

– Robert IsaacsFounder / CEO, Nine Minds

Nine Minds also built a Huntress emulator so they could test the integration without depending on live incidents. They told us a dedicated sandbox environment would make that easier, and we've shared that feedback with our team.

What Else Can You Build?

AlgaPSA's integration shows one common pattern: pull incidents from Huntress and turn them into tickets. But the API supports a lot more.

A few examples:

Get incidents in real time. Instead of polling, Huntress Webhooks push incidents and escalations to your PSA, Slack, or SIEM as they happen.

Act on incidents. Approve or reject remediations through the Incident Report response API, and isolate or release hosts through the Agents API.

Automate onboarding. Create, update, and delete organizations programmatically. For example, when a new client is added in your RMM, automation can create the matching Huntress organization and start EDR deployment.

Reconcile billing and build reports. Pull billing reports and per-product organization stats, like agent counts, SIEM storage, and ITDR identity counts, into your dashboards, QBRs, or PSA contracts.

Bring Huntress into AI workflows. The Huntress MCP server connects your AI assistant to your incidents, agents, billing data, and more.

Prefer to see how this works? Watch our video below to see inside the Huntress API, Webooks, and MCP server:

Ready to Learn More?

AlgaPSA's integration started with a customer request and ended with a shipped feature just a few days later. That's the kind of experience we want every developer to have with the Huntress API. If you've been thinking about connecting Huntress to your own tools, the docs are a good place to start.

Build on the Huntress API: Start with the Huntress API docs.

Use Huntress with AlgaPSA: See the AlgaPSA Huntress integration docs for setup steps.

Share feedback: Have an idea for an endpoint, webhook, or integration? Add it to our Integrations, Webhooks, and APIs feedback board.

articles.full_text:
In November 2015, we released our first in-house macOS sandbox, Box of Apples, followed by an update in March 2018 that introduced HTML behavior reports, desktop screenshots, and process trees. Over the past decade, the macOS ecosystem and the threat landscape targeting it have changed dramatically. Apple transitioned its hardware architecture from Intel (x86_64) to Apple Silicon (ARM64), hardened its operating system security model, and deprecated legacy dynamic tracing mechanisms. At the same time, macOS threat actors have shifted toward native ARM64 binaries, multi-stage social engineering installers, credential-harvesting AppleScripts, and evasive infostealers.

Today, we are excited to introduce macOS Mirage, our brand-new, ground-up dynamic analysis sandbox built natively for Apple Silicon and macOS 26. macOS Mirage replaces Box of Apples as part of the VirusTotal Multi-Sandbox project, delivering high-fidelity behavioral telemetry, automated Sigma behavioral detections mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, and—exclusively within our Private Scanning product offering—full Interactive Live Analysis.

Why We Built macOS Mirage: Beyond Box of Apples

Box of Apples was designed for an era of Intel-based Macs and relied on dtrace scripts to monitor system calls. As macOS evolved, two structural shifts required a completely new approach:

Native Apple Silicon (ARM64) Execution: Modern macOS applications and malware families are compiled natively for Apple Silicon or distributed as Universal Mach-O binaries. Running modern samples on legacy Intel hardware either fails outright or misses architecture-specific execution paths. macOS Mirage runs natively on bare-metal Apple Silicon hardware with Apple's native virtualization stack and macOS 26, ensuring authentic execution fidelity.

Modern Kernel-Backed Behavioral Telemetry: In modern macOS releases, System Integrity Protection (SIP) restricts legacy dtrace hooks, and high syscall volumes could cause event drops. macOS Mirage uses modern, kernel-supported macOS security instrumentation to capture process creation, command-line arguments, file system modifications, persistence installation, and access to sensitive credential stores without losing events.

Capability

Box of Apples (2015 / 2018)

macOS Mirage (2026)

Hardware Architecture

Intel (x86_64)

Native Apple Silicon (ARM64)

Operating System

OS X 10.11 El Capitan / 10.13 High Sierra

Modern macOS (including macOS 26)

Supported Payloads

Intel Mach-O bundles and basic installers

ARM64 & Universal Mach-O, .dmg, .pkg, .app, .sh, .py, PDFs

Behavioral Telemetry

Legacy dtrace syscall tracing

Modern kernel-supported security telemetry & accurate process trees

Behavioral Detections

Basic behavior tags

Sigma behavioral rules, MITRE ATT&CK mapping, and YARA scanning

Dropped File Analysis

Basic file list

Automated extraction and recursive multi-engine scanning of dropped payloads

Network Capabilities

Basic NAT egress

Multi-mode networking (Internet, Simulated INetSim, HTTPS MITM, Tor, VPN) (Private Scanning exclusive)

Interactive Control

Automated execution only

Live Mouse, Keyboard & Clipboard Control (Private Scanning exclusive)

Rich GUI Execution and Persistence Tracking

Many macOS samples package their payloads inside disk images (.dmg) or application bundles (.app) that initialize graphical windows, register background services, or trigger system notifications during execution. macOS Mirage provides full graphics acceleration and desktop monitoring, capturing both visual screenshots and underlying system modifications in real time.

Figure 1: Dynamic detonation of a macOS application in macOS Mirage, capturing both the application GUI and a macOS system notification alerting to a newly registered persistent background Login Item.

Figure 2: Full window management, 3D rendering, and Dock process tracking inside macOS Mirage.

In addition to capturing screenshots to show what a user would see on screen, macOS Mirage automatically monitors security-sensitive locations across the operating system, including:

Persistence Mechanisms: LaunchAgents, LaunchDaemons, Login Items, and cron jobs.

Shell & Environment Profiles: Modifications to .zshrc, .bashrc, .zshenv, and /etc/profile.

Credential & Privacy Stores: Unauthorized access to Keychain databases (login.keychain-db), browser cookie and credential stores, SSH keys, and the Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC.db) database.

System & Network Configuration: Changes to /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, and /private/etc/sudoers.

New Behavioral Detections with Sigma Rules: Catching a macOS Info-Stealer in Action

To help analysts quickly identify malicious behavior without sifting through thousands of raw file and process events, macOS Mirage evaluates runtime telemetry against a curated library of macOS Sigma rules and maps every detection directly to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.

Let's look at a real-world example of a macOS info-stealer and credential-phishing sample analyzed by macOS Mirage on VirusTotal: be77bca22f078d57058535ddcf26a39a752a8df030392cb45ba6a60e06651878

When executed inside macOS Mirage, the binary (unix51436504) performs a multi-stage credential theft and persistence chain:

AppleScript Password Phishing: The malware invokes /usr/bin/osascript to display a deceptive system prompt titled "Password Request" asking the user: "Please enter device password to continue."

Local Credential Validation & LaunchDaemon Persistence: It validates the harvested password against local Directory Services (dscl . authonly) and invokes sudo -S to copy /tmp/daemonplist to /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.somedaemon.plist.

articles.full_text:
The British government has announced a range of new initiatives designed to better protect the nation from emerging AI threats.

Speaking at Imperial College London on October 12, AI minister Kanishka Narayan laid out a series of plans, including the use of frontier models to find vulnerabilities in government systems.

“Our central vulnerability-monitoring service has already helped reduce the time taken to fix identified weaknesses from 50 days to just eight. Built on these advances, I want us to go further,” he explained.

“I am announcing that the DCMS cyber minister, the security minister and I will lead the urgent use of frontier AI capabilities to find weaknesses within government systems before attackers exploit them, protect essential government systems, and respond more effectively to emerging threats.”

This follows a series of internal hackathons run by the Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) where frontier AI was used to find over 400 software flaws in public sector IT which were subsequently patched.

Read more on government AI efforts: UK Government Launches AI Safety Scheme to Tackle Deepfakes.

Narayan also announced that the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and the AI Security Institute (AISI) would work together to “develop robust ways” to respond to and contain agentic AI incidents.

That follows a series of cases in which frontier models have hacked organizations, including governments, during testing.

Additionally, security minister, Dan Jarvis, will lead a “cross-government program to strengthen our defenses against cyber-attacks, including from AI,” Narayan explained.

A National Cyber Action Plan will be published “soon,” he added.

There will also be amendments to the long-awaited Cyber Security and Resilience Bill (CSRB) to help protect organizations from “loss-of-control” risks and AI-powered threats.

“That includes identifying and reporting on serious incidents and near misses, including reducing AI-driven risk across essential services, and ensuring serious AI incidents can be properly reviewed,” Narayan said.

AISI Testing of Frontier Models Resumes

While many of the details related to these initiatives are still being worked out, there was at least confirmation of one positive development from the AI minister.

He revealed that the AISI has resumed testing of frontier models including Gemini 4 Argon, to help better inform model developers and the global community of emerging risks. The Trump administration had previously blocked access to such models by any testing bodies outside the US.

Narayan said that, in the future, the UK could extend this expertise and draw on its heritage in semiconductor design to nurture new capabilities in AI verification. This nascent field will help to ensure AI, and the outputs of models, comply with rules, regulations and safety standards.

Okta field CTO, EMEA, Richard Wainwright, welcomed the focus on AI security and called for kill switches to be considered as part of the CSRB.

“As AI agents become more autonomous, safety must be built into the infrastructure UK businesses and government rely on,” he added. “Everyone wants a 'big red button' to turn off rogue AI agents.”

Carla Baker, senior director of UK policy at Palo Alto Networks, praised the government's focus on proactive threat detection and incident reporting, arguing that adversaries are deploying AI “at scale” in attacks to accelerate intrusions and exfiltration.

"Defense must enable progress, not cause paralysis. Building national resilience isn't about imposing heavy-handed regulation that stifles UK competitiveness,” she continued. “By combining practical, robust security guardrails with the operational agility that organizations need, the UK can safely deploy frontier AI and win on the global stage."

The success of a mandatory incident reporting regime will depend on which organizations it would cover, what counts as “frontier” and how “incidents” are defined, added Manifold Security CEO, Neal Swaelens.

“Given we’re seeing time and time again that incidents of agentic AI breaches are being reported months after they occurred, if mandatory reporting is to have any impact, it must be paired with observability, including proper oversight of what agents are doing at runtime so that incidents can be caught when they happen, and not weeks later,” he argued.

“OpenAI’s agent in Australia's Medicare portal, for example, took months to be detected and disclosed.”

articles.full_text:
Today, Silverfort announces an integration that brings its runtime Identity Security approach to Agent Gateway, part of Google Cloud Gemini Enterprise, giving teams real-time visibility into AI agent activity and enforcing access decisions as they happen.

After Silverfort was named in Google Cloud’s Next ’26 announcement among the partner services bringing identity and governance administration to Agent Gateway, it is time to announce the new milestone we have been building toward, and it lands at exactly the moment enterprises need it.

A milestone for securing agentic AI

Agent Gateway is a genuinely significant piece of infrastructure. Announced in preview at Google Cloud Next ’26, it provides “an open, extensible, scalable way to enforce centralized governance policies to securely connect agents, models, and tools across runtimes.”

For an Identity Security company, that is exciting news. Every agent interaction can be configured to flow through Agent Gateway, which makes it the natural place to apply Identity Security controls at scale. Silverfort now secures the AI agents running there by connecting directly into the platform’s control plane, so agent owners never have to route traffic through a separate gateway.

Why AI agents change the identity problem

Organizations are adopting AI agents faster than most identity and security teams can inventory, monitor, or control them. These agents authenticate into systems, access sensitive data, and take actions across cloud and SaaS environments, often with broad privileges and limited oversight. The result is a rapidly expanding identity attack surface that traditional security tools were not built to address.

Agents also do not fit neatly into traditional security models. Unlike a human user who logs in once and works within predictable patterns, agents can chain actions across services, escalate broadly privileged credentials and tools, and behave in ways that are difficult to predict or trace. That leaves most organizations unable to answer basic questions: how many agents are running, who owns them, what they can access, and which ones are overprivileged.

These risks also arrive from two directions at once. Alongside the exposure created by an organization’s own agents, adversaries are now using AI-powered attack models built to probe, exploit, and move laterally at machine speed. They are not the same problem, but they converge on one control plane: what an identity is permitted to access, and what it is allowed to do. When agents are overprivileged and attackers are autonomous, the window to act is very small.

What Silverfort delivers on Agent Gateway

Visibility into agent activity

Silverfort automatically discovers AI agents operating through Agent Gateway and maps each one back to its human owner for clear accountability. Security teams get a complete view of agent behavior, ownership, permissions, and access paths across Google Cloud and beyond.

Runtime enforcement controls

Silverfort evaluates agent requests against access policies at the Agent Gateway layer before they reach downstream systems, limiting unauthorized privilege escalation and risky agent overreach. If an agent attempts to access a dataset, SaaS application, or internal resource outside its approved permissions, Silverfort evaluates that request in real time and enforces the appropriate policy response. Unauthorized attempts are stopped in line rather than detected after the fact.

Risk-based prioritization

Not all agents carry the same level of risk. Silverfort analyzes agent exposure based on privilege level, access patterns, and connections to sensitive resources. Overprivileged agents, dormant credentials, and high-risk access paths are flagged and prioritized so teams can focus remediation where it matters most.

Granular access policies and detailed audit trails

Policies are defined by agent identity, target application, and action type, and are managed from a centralized dashboard. Access requests are allowed or blocked in real time, and all agent activity is auditable and tied to enterprise identity governance frameworks and to the human using the agent.

Because the controls sit where agent traffic already flows, organizations gain all of this without deploying additional infrastructure or redesigning how their agents are built. Developers keep building. Agents keep running.

Meeting agents where they actually run

AI agents do not all run the same way, so Silverfort delivers runtime enforcement in two complementary ways. The Silverfort MCP Gateway is a universal inline enforcement layer between agents and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers they access, built for custom and open-framework agents operating outside closed, vendor-specific ecosystems.

By connecting directly into the control plane of leading agentic platforms, Silverfort enforces policy without requiring agent owners to route traffic through a separate gateway. That’s the right fit for cloud-managed enterprise environments where scale, platform resilience, and zero workflow disruption are critical.

An expanded collaboration with Google Cloud

The Agent Gateway integration is not Silverfort’s only collaboration with Google Cloud. In June, Silverfort launched an integration with Google Security Operations that pulls live identity risk into SecOps playbooks and pushes enforcement back the other way, letting analysts raise a user’s risk indicator or tighten a service account policy from inside a response case. It ships through the Google Cloud partner integrations catalog.

Both integrations point in the same direction: identity telemetry and runtime enforcement reaching Google Cloud teams inside the tools they already run.

One platform for human, machine, and AI agent identities

AI agents do not operate in isolation. They share access paths with human users, service accounts, and other non-human identities, and they often create overlapping risk across all of them. A compromised or overprivileged agent can become a path to lateral movement, privilege escalation, or data exposure, and protecting the agent alone without visibility into the identities around it leaves gaps that attackers will find.

Silverfort brings AI agents into the same Identity Security Platform used to protect human and non-human identities across cloud and on-premises environments. Because those controls apply at runtime, they hold against both pressures – an agent drifting outside its approved scope, and an attacker moving at machine speed with credentials it should never have been able to use. Enterprises rarely run a single agentic AI platform, and enforcement extends across the wider ecosystem regardless of where agents run.

Availability

The Silverfort integration with Google Cloud’s Agent Gateway is now live. Organizations running AI agents on Google Cloud can get started without installing additional software or making code changes to existing workflows. Visibility and runtime protection begin on day one.

This is the beginning

Agentic AI is moving from experimentation to production faster than any enterprise technology in recent memory, and identity is where its security will be decided. Bringing runtime Identity Security to Agent Gateway is a significant step, and one of many we intend to take as the agentic ecosystem grows.

Today, Recorded Future is announcing AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists, curated datasets for security teams to identify, monitor, and implement controls for AI-related network traffic. AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists are included for free for Recorded Future customers with a Cyber Operations license.

Artificial intelligence has increasingly become enterprise infrastructure and organizations are now confronting unsanctioned tool use (also known as shadow AI), data exposure, and autonomous behavior that their controls cannot always see.

Recorded Future's AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists focus on closing this gap across risk, IT, and GRC teams whether the goal is policy enforcement, data loss prevention, or detecting shadow AI.

AI is accumulating security debt

The hidden risks of an abundance of AI within an organization are often overshadowed by the daily threats that have to be prioritized by a security team. Last year, we reported on how security debt has been accrued by almost every organization, and the unaddressed risks are piling up faster than teams can service them. As a result, blind spots in AI governance are also increasing.

Take, for example, agentic AI. Its adoption is accelerating rapidly and agents are operating across interconnected systems, giving threat actors more room to exploit vulnerabilities at the organizational level and across supply chains.

Consider a free, viral AI assistant that an employee discovers on social media and installs on their own machine to boost productivity. No procurement process, no security review, no IT visibility.

That's not a hypothetical. OpenClaw, a free open-source AI assistant, saw explosive adoption earlier this year with almost no organizational oversight. Multiply that across a workforce and security teams left trying to govern tools they don't know exist.

By 2027, an estimated 75% of employees are expected to adopt or build technology outside IT governance. As agents become more ubiquitous, defenders need to ensure they can identify which technologies are living on their networks, and begin to track and manage access permissions for autonomous processes in the same way they manage permissions for human users.

Introducing AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists

While many threat feeds give you a wall of indicators and leave you to figure out what they are and whether to trust them, Recorded Future’s AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists do the opposite.

AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists are curated, regularly refreshed datasets that map the AI infrastructure your users, developers, and adversaries are actually reaching for. articles.title: Wait, Did We Just Invent Classifiers Again? Introducing Jev, a new way to do AI.
articles.context: This week TypeSafe AI launched a new kind of model, called Jev, and it’s very interesting
articles.full_text:
For the last few years, when somebody says “AI,” what they are usually referring to is a Large Language Model, or LLM for short. You chuck some text in, it has a think, and it gives you some more text back. This is brilliant if you want code written, documents summarised, or quantum physics explained to you in a limerick, but while this is great for humans, most software doesn’t actually want a beautifully written paragraph. Software just wants an answer so it can make a decision. Is this event suspicious? Should I escalate it? Is this high risk? Which workflow should deal with it? For this, LLMs aren’t really the ideal tool of choice. This is all about to change.

This week TypeSafe AI launched a new kind of model, called Jev, and it’s very interesting. This AI model doesn’t want to have a conversation with you – you cannot use it conversationally. Jev is just trying to do one thing, and it wants to do that one thing well: It’s trying to decide.

So, what is Jev exactly?

Jev is what TypeSafe calls a “System One” model. Rather than primarily generating a sequence of tokens like a traditional LLM, you give Jev some state (think datapoints), define questions about that state (what you want to know), and tell it what valid answers look like (to format the output). Jev then interprets all your inputs, does some smart things, and returns probabilistic decisions. So rather than asking an LLM, “Can you analyse this security event and tell me what you think?,” you can ask Jev for substantially more specific things like: Is this likely malicious? Does this warrant investigation? Is credential compromise likely? How severe is it? What is great is that you can define those outputs beforehand. You’re asking for a decision, rather than hoping the model eventually buries one somewhere inside three paragraphs of text.

Now before anybody says anything, I know what you’re thinking: “Hang on, haven’t we just invented classifiers again?” I had the same reaction. If you’ve never head of a classifier, this is what we used to use before everybody decided their product desperately needed a chatbot glued to the side of it. Machine learning was full of classifiers: Spam or not spam? Fraud or legitimate? Malware or benign? Cat or, tragically, not cat? Classifiers were incredibly useful, but normally quite narrow. You needed training data, labels, pipelines, and usually a model built specifically for that problem. Generative AI gave us something far more flexible because we could suddenly describe what we wanted in natural language. Jev feels a bit like taking that semantic understanding and putting it back inside the old classifier model, but with significantly more accessibility.

The real-world approach: Jev in action with Cato

Let’s use Jev for something a little more interesting than asking whether an ice cream sandwich is technically a sandwich, using the the TypeSafe Playground. Let’s use Jev to interpret data taken from the Cato Management Application via the EventsFeed API.

We will start with a deliberately boring question: a finance employee in the UK, using their normal managed laptop, was successfully authenticating with MFA and downloading four files from SharePoint during the working day. All this extracted information from our API will populate the ‘State’ field – this is the current state of the query, and it should represent what we want to interpret. We then can add a few “Questions” to the field below, as we want to specify a formatted output:

The questions asked were not difficult for a human, but very difficult for a traditional LLM to give a succinct answer due to generative analysis:

Does this require investigation?

Is it likely malicious?

Is credential compromise likely?

What should the security response be?

How severe is the risk?

Instead of producing a 300-page AI slop security report, Jev instead evaluates those individual decisions and responds with probabilities of likelihood. After clicking the “Run” button to process the query, Jev outputted the following:

So far, lovely. This event doesn’t need investigation, and Jev believes that there should be a 100% probability that this incident should be closed. There is a 5% chance that this could be likely malicious, but the correlated signals overall indicate that the current state of the event is benign. Fantastic – but what if we did something a little more interesting, like changing the state of the event? After all, the state of your users (and network) is always changing.

We will now use the same user, application, and questions. Except now the device state has changed. The device is now unknown and unmanaged, the connection is coming from Russia (22 minutes after a UK session), it’s 3:17 in the morning, there are impossible-travel indicators, and instead of downloading four files from SharePoint, our finance user has just hoovered up 1,847 documents from Finance and M&A folders. In technical security terminology: that looks a bit dodgy, but these are all parameters we can extract via the Cato API to help Jev make a judgement call.

After hitting Run again, Jev reprocessed the input and a different decision was output based on the evidence provided. This model was able process the data feed and reclassify this not as a benign event that should be instantly closed, but instead the user should be “Contained” as there’s enough evidence to imply a device compromise with 99% certainty.

This capability is incredibly awesome. We have given it the same questions and same output structure, but with a different state of the world and different decisions. I haven’t overcomplicated the process by asking the model to become my SOC analyst 0; instead it’s just used the power of AI to help me accelerate my business decisions. ChatGPT would attempt write an incident report, create a ticket, isolate the device, burn $40k in tokens, and notify somebody on Slack, but this isn’t what most companies want. I’ve asked Jev to perform the fuzzy bit: make a semantic judgement. This output can then actually drive business decisions.

Normal software can then do the boring bit, and boring is rather lovely (and desired) when it comes to security. Imagine a world where a Jev decision greater than 90% confidence automatically creates an investigation. Perhaps 60–90% confidence rate automatically triggers a human review. Perhaps a combination of credential compromise and high severity triggers another workflow; the model provides the judgement and deterministic controls decide what that judgement is actually allowed to do.

Models like Jev are the next logical evolution in business process automation – where we start to leverage AI not to just provide a fuzzy output, but instead provide an actionable decision and output to accelerate your business. The probability percentage could drive accountability, while also retaining control. This is very important when we consider the current “rogue” nature of AI we hear in the news.

Secure, Contain, Protect.

If you’re still reading, I believe that what we are seeing here goes beyond Jev itself, but Jev is the starting point of re-taking control from the chaos of our current software landscape. AI is starting to disappear inside applications, with embedded AI being the bane of most organisations. It won’t always announce itself with a giant “Ask AI” button. Models today increasingly make tiny decisions inside APIs, workflows, agents, and applications, often without the end user even realising an AI model was involved. For security teams, that should set a few alarm bells ringing, as you are no longer in the driving seat when it comes to your applications and their output.

Today if organisations only monitor visits to ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, they’re going to miss a huge part of what AI adoption is becoming. You need to understand where AI is being used, which models and services your organisation is communicating with, what data is being sent to them, and what those AI-driven decisions can cause downstream.

The classifier might be back. But this time it could be buried absolutely everywhere. Your job now is to make sure you can see it, govern it, and apply controls without impacting your user experience. For this, Cato Networks can help.
